Energy has long sat at the intersection of public good and private enterprise, a critical area where governments have a natural stake, but valuable enough that markets do too. That balance has shifted back and forth for generations. Over the past decade, however, the scale and scope of government interventions have increased, particularly in economies traditionally built on free-market principles.The number of industrial policy interventions by governments in advanced economies, predominantly in the US and Europe, has nearly tripled over the past decade. The result is a level of policy whiplash and fragmentation that has made planning for capital-intensive sectors like energy a growing challenge.Businesses feel this volatility every day, but awareness isn’t the problem. Most companies monitor policy, yet the insights gained are rarely substantially integrated into capital allocation or wider strategy. Few companies engage in edge case scenario modeling, and even fewer have signposts in place alerting them to when a particular signal demands action. Changes in policy changes may be monitored, but most companies lack the capabilities needed to incorporate these insights into the planning process, let alone give them a seat at the table where decisions are made. That gap becomes a competitor’s advantage.This article explains why many organizations haven’t kept pace with increasing government interventions, the five policy capabilities that set leaders apart, and the first steps executives can take to put this best practice framework into action.The New Policy Reality
An industrial policy intervention is a focused government action that plausibly reshapes the competitive environment. This can involve targeting specific industries directly or reshaping market conditions such as vehicle emission targets, carbon pricing, trade policies such as sanctions and tariffs, and energy tax credits and subsidies.Thanks to growing government intervention, the policy environment for energy, industrial, and other capital-intensive businesses has become increasingly uncertain. This uncertainty shows up across three elements: how often governments intervene, how quickly they change course, and the kinds of interventions they carry out.The first driver of uncertainty is frequency. Total government interventions covering industrial policy have nearly tripled since 2015, surpassing 11,000 in 2024 and 2025 combined, predominately in advanced economies. (See Exhibit 1.) Energy and energy-intensive sectors account for roughly 65% of that activity. While the share of intervention into energy-related industries is historically consistent, what has changed is their scale.

Next is the sheer speed of policy reversals and other major changes, which can create a sense of policy whiplash. For example, it took just 35 months for the US to introduce and then largely unwind Inflation Reduction Act subsidies. The EU was still issuing implementation rules for its Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) 16 days before its binding phase began. (See Exhibit 2.)

The third driver is scope. Governments are increasingly reaching for more interventionist tools, from local content requirements to a more direct government role in energy supply and procurement. A decade ago, governments rationalized many interventions based on climate and sustainability goals. Today, the focus is often sovereignty and security, and that justification could easily shift again.New research from BCG’s Center for Energy Impact (CEI) and Center for Sustainability Policy & Regulation confirms that executives feel this volatility acutely. More than 85% of the 150 executives surveyed say that both policy and the geopolitical landscape are less predictable now than five to ten years ago. Policy reversals that once took years now happen within a single investment cycle. And given the heightened level of geopolitical friction and interconnected global supply chains, regulatory shifts and trade policy changes in one jurisdiction often reshape economics elsewhere across the globe. Changes also ripple throughout the value chain, with suppliers, customers, and financing partners all forced to recalibrate as policy shifts.The financial stakes have risen accordingly. CEI forecasts that capital expenditures from 275 of the world’s largest energy companies will reach $7.5 trillion between 2026 and 2030, around 25% higher than the past five years. At that scale, exposure runs both ways, as the same policy shift that strands one company’s assets can hand a competitor a windfall.

Internal Fragmentation
In today’s environment, policy is no longer a background constraint that government affairs teams can manage in isolation. It is as material to a project’s economics as input costs and needs to be evaluated with the same rigor. Yet just 19% of the executives surveyed say policy is fully embedded in their investment decisions, and two-thirds report that they are revising or reversing major decisions more often than before. Most companies still plan on the relatively short three- to five-year cycles that often match political terms, and they don’t often assess policy across their assets’ time horizons of 40 years or more.

In today’s environment, policy is as material to a project’s economics as input costs and needs to be evaluated with the same rigor.

Moreover, policy expertise is often disconnected from the parts of the business that make decisions. Government relations teams lead advocacy and watch the policy environment most closely; however, while around 70% of surveyed executives say their government affairs teams monitor policy, only 12% report that the same team analyzes policy’s commercial impact. (See Exhibit 3.) And despite its central role in capital allocation, the finance function typically engages the least of any other area across monitoring, anticipating change, and making recommendations. In other cases, developing commercial policy insight is fragmented across many teams, meaning that each team may interpret policy signals differently, with no forum to reconcile the view and act in unison.

The biggest reported capability gaps confirm that most executives lack the ability to keep pace with how quickly policy issues change. Around 66% of respondents reported that they struggle to develop early warning signals for policy changes and track them in real time, and 52% do not have scenario-planning capabilities. More than 40% report that they have no clear internal pathway to respond once a signal is spotted. That gap means even well-monitored risks can go unaddressed. (See Exhibit 4.) Closing these gaps is exactly where leaders pull ahead.

Five Capability Dimensions That Define the Leaders
Agility in the face of rapid policy change is not enabled simply through bigger government affairs departments or deeper relations with government. Drawing on our survey and interviews with leaders of energy and energy-intensive companies across the US and Europe, our research shows that competitive advantage comes from changing how the entire organization engages with policy, across five dimensions (see Exhibit 5).

Leaders assess the full landscape. Those companies that best respond to policy volatility have moved beyond tracking only those policies with direct impact. They now build AI-enabled tools that map the full regulatory landscape, including indirect effects, across the entire asset portfolio and supply chain in every relevant market. These tools also monitor community sentiment, as it too shapes a project’s ability to proceed. All teams that keep track of or analyze policy must compare exposures and bring up disagreements about how policy affects the overall strategy. Gaps between different functions’ perceptions are often where mutual understanding breaks down if there is no agreed-on holistic company view.Leaders quantify exposure rigorously. Analyzing the potential impacts of pricing policy on capex, P&L, and net present value is table stakes. What sets leaders apart is tracing second-order effects, such as how a policy shift ripples through the supply chain and affects other stakeholders, and stress-testing options. They also recognize that much like policy, optionality has a cost. The flexibility to delay a decision, change a supplier, hedge against a scenario, or reverse course isn’t always without cost, and leading companies figure that cost into their decisions.Leaders simulate over the horizon. Leaders have shifted away from planning around the outcome of the next election to building scenarios that look ahead ten or more years. Each scenario is granular and regularly tested against edge cases and extreme conditions, giving leaders a strategic portfolio of options with built-in on- and off-ramps. This lets leaders separate which actions are scenario-dependent from the no-brainers that hold true regardless of outcome. They distinguish reversible from irreversible capital commitments in scenarios, so an exit can be a preplanned move, not a reactive crisis.Leaders track with commercial precision. Rather than simply monitoring headline developments and regulatory filings, these companies build AI-enabled tools to identify and track signposts of change. Live signals are scored, escalated, and tied directly to the prebuilt scenario playbook. They watch for emergent issues, not just the developments already on their radar, and track softer signals, including community sentiment. This shows which stage gate they’ve reached across their scenarios, and when it’s time to pivot ahead of policy change rather than just keep watching.Leaders integrate across the enterprise. These companies have progressed from allowing policy insights to sit within one function to ensuring that they drive every capital, sourcing, product, and site decision. Policy analysis stops being a side report from one team and instead becomes a required step for everyone: no major decision can go to the C-suite unless it has first been comprehensively assessed for a range of policy pathways and risks. The same discipline applies to external engagement. Traditional channels to government are important, but they no longer capture the full picture. Leaders also build relationships through partnerships and industry coalitions and actively work to build trust and positive community engagement. This allows action to be taken quickly if the policy and political environment changes.These five capabilities pay off when it’s time to act. Offshore wind developers that had kept their options open on major investments, for example, were able to exit quickly and pivot to other opportunities when the US government froze offshore wind permits in 2025. Similarly, global automakers that had long hedged across multiple vehicle powertrains, supported by close tracking of regulations in their many markets, weren’t overexposed when the US federal electric vehicle tax credit expired that same year. In both cases, the advantage wasn’t just predicting the outcome but being ready to act quickly to overcome uncertainty.Act Before the Next Cycle Turns
There are no indications that current policy volatility will slow any time soon. Because energy sector investment timelines stretch over multiple decades, reacting to individual administration or political cycles is a losing strategy. As one energy executive put it, a company that only monitors policy has already failed, not just because it misses risk, but because it misses the upside that competitors capture first.Embed policy expertise deeper into the organization and strategy. Most companies have several teams tracking or assessing impacts of policy, each in its own silo. Bring them together into one holistic company-wide view and feed this back into every major decision.Run more frequent, granular scenario testing. Move beyond periodic, short-term assessments based on the current political cycle. Test plans against a wide range of policy outcomes, including the edge cases (both upside and downside). Use new AI tools to build signposts that flag changes early when it’s time to pivot to a different scenario or pathway.Build optionality into the process that takes you from the project funnel through to the final investment decision. Ensure there is a diverse range of strategic market opportunities considered, as well as optionality at the project level. This could include diversified options for suppliers and commercial offtake, and ensuring infrastructure investment can pivot between fuel sources and technologies. Optionality isn’t free, but the cost of having none when policy shifts is almost always higher.The Bottom Line
Policy volatility is two-sided. The same shifts that strand some companies’ investments create windfalls for others that are positioned ahead of the change. The difference is rarely sector, scale, or luck. It’s capability.Enhanced policy capabilities are now a source of durable competitive advantage. Companies that are proactive and build in systematic optionality will make better capital decisions by understanding all options and risks, and they’ll be able to respond to policy shifts as preplanned moves rather than crises. Those that remain in reactive mode will continue to absorb the downside, whether through inaction or by following slowly after faster competitors.The window to build this advantage will not stay open indefinitely. Every investment cycle that passes without an updated policy capability embedded in decision making is a cycle during which faster-moving peers extend their lead. The companies that start now will be the hardest to displace when the next policy cycle turns.
